title: Research
text:
Aims:
Integrate field investigations with remote sensing to reveal cross-scale mechanisms, support the development of robust model to improve forest management for enhanced human well-being.


Forest above ground biomass estimation
How to estimate forest AGB across large spatial scale?

LiDAR-based modeling of forest above-ground biomass (AGB) using USGS 3DEP and NEON airborne point clouds, integrated with GEDI spaceborne LiDAR footprints and ESA CCI Biomass products for cross-scale validation. Built a large-scale processing pipeline that derives canopy structure metrics (height percentiles, density, rumple index) and predicts plot-level AGB with Random Forest, XGBoost, LightGBM, and stacked ensemble models, evaluated with grouped cross-validation and SHAP-based interpretation.
Tools: R (lidR, lasR, terra, sf), Python (scikit-learn, XGBoost, LightGBM, SHAP)



Cooling effect of urban green space
How does the urban green space regulate the temperature?

Quantifying how the structure and composition of urban green spaces moderate land surface temperature across cities. Integrates USGS 3DEP airborne LiDAR-derived canopy metrics (height, cover, vertical complexity) with land cover and satellite-derived LST to model cooling magnitude as a function of canopy structure, patch geometry, and surrounding impervious context.
Tools: R (lidR, terra, sf, lme4), Python (xarray, rasterio, scikit-learn)


Forest Loss Analysis
How to accurately detect the forest loss and what is their relationship to climate change?

1: How forest disturbance Quantifying forest loss trends and drivers across large spatial extents using time-series satellite imagery. The workflow integrates Hansen Global Forest Change data with climate and topographic covariates to attribute disturbance to fire, harvest, and insect outbreak.
Tools: R, Google Earth Engine, tidyverse








Note



More projects and reproducible notebooks will be added here over time.

title: Downloading and Analyzing GEDI L4A Above-Ground Biomass Data
text:
Setup

install.packages(c("rGEDI", "hdf5r", "sf", "terra",
                   "ggplot2", "dplyr", "leaflet", "viridis", "patchwork"))


library(hdf5r); library(sf); library(terra)
library(ggplot2); library(dplyr); library(leaflet)
library(viridis); library(patchwork); library(scales)

title: Downloading and Analyzing GEDI L4A Above-Ground Biomass Data
text:
Step 1 — Define Two Study Areas

# ── Region 1: NEON SCBI, Front Royal, VA ─────────────────────────────────
scbi <- list(
  name    = "NEON SCBI — Front Royal, VA",
  lon_min = -78.20, lat_min = 38.85,
  lon_max = -78.10, lat_max = 38.95
)

# ── Region 2: Central Park & surrounding urban area, NYC ─────────────────
nyc <- list(
  name    = "Central Park & surroundings — New York City",
  lon_min = -74.05, lat_min = 40.70,
  lon_max = -73.85, lat_max = 40.85
)

region_to_sf <- function(r) {
  st_bbox(c(xmin = r$lon_min, ymin = r$lat_min,
            xmax = r$lon_max, ymax = r$lat_max),
          crs = 4326) |> st_as_sfc() |> st_as_sf()
}

The map below shows the GEDI orbital track coverage (green lines) over both study areas (red bounding boxes). Ascending (SW→NE) and descending (NW→SE) passes cross due to the ISS orbital inclination of ~51.6°.

title: Downloading and Analyzing GEDI L4A Above-Ground Biomass Data
text:
Step 2 — Find GEDI L4A Granules

library(httr); library(jsonlite)

gedi_finder <- function(r) {
  url  <- paste0("https://lpdaacsvc.cr.usgs.gov/services/gedifinder",
                 "?product=GEDI04_A&version=002",
                 "&bbox=", r$lon_min, ",", r$lat_min,
                 ",",      r$lon_max, ",", r$lat_max)
  fromJSON(content(GET(url), "text"))$data
}

scbi_granules <- gedi_finder(scbi)
nyc_granules  <- gedi_finder(nyc)

cat("SCBI granules:", length(scbi_granules), "\n")
cat("NYC  granules:", length(nyc_granules),  "\n")

title: Downloading and Analyzing GEDI L4A Above-Ground Biomass Data
text:
Step 3 — Download Granules
Requires a free NASA EarthData account (urs.earthdata.nasa.gov).

library(rGEDI)
gediDownload(filepath = scbi_granules, outdir = "data/gedi_scbi")
gediDownload(filepath = nyc_granules,  outdir = "data/gedi_nyc")


Each granule is ~500 MB–2 GB. For a small bounding box, typically 1–3 granules suffice.

quality_filter <- function(df) {
  df |> filter(quality == 1, degrade == 0, agbd >= 0, agbd < 1000)
}

scbi_clean <- quality_filter(scbi_raw)
nyc_clean  <- quality_filter(nyc_raw)

title: Downloading and Analyzing GEDI L4A Above-Ground Biomass Data
text:
Results
The figures below show processed GEDI L4A output for both regions.

Spatial Distribution of AGBD
Each point represents one GEDI footprint (~25 m diameter). Colors encode AGBD in Mg/ha.


SCBI shows dense, continuous forest cover with high AGBD (100–400 Mg/ha). The NYC panel reveals a strong spatial contrast between the vegetated core of Central Park (higher AGBD) and the surrounding impervious urban fabric (near-zero AGBD).




AGBD Frequency Distribution


SCBI follows a right-skewed log-normal distribution typical of mature temperate forest. NYC shows a strongly bimodal pattern: a large spike near zero (impervious surfaces, sparse street trees) and a secondary mode around 80–130 Mg/ha (park tree canopy).




AGBD Violin + Box Plot




NYC Detail — Central Park vs Urban Surroundings
GEDI footprints are classified by whether they fall inside the Central Park boundary (~-73.981 to -73.949 lon, 40.764 to 40.800 lat):

title: Downloading and Analyzing GEDI L4A Above-Ground Biomass Data
text:
Step 6 — Rasterize to 500 m Grid

rasterize_agbd <- function(df, region, res = 0.0045) {
  r_tmpl <- rast(xmin = region$lon_min, xmax = region$lon_max,
                 ymin = region$lat_min, ymax = region$lat_max,
                 resolution = res, crs = "EPSG:4326")
  vect(df, geom = c("lon", "lat"), crs = "EPSG:4326") |>
    rasterize(r_tmpl, field = "agbd", fun = "mean")
}

r_scbi <- rasterize_agbd(scbi_clean, scbi)
r_nyc  <- rasterize_agbd(nyc_clean,  nyc)

par(mfrow = c(1, 2))
plot(r_scbi, col = hcl.colors(100, "viridis"),
     main = "SCBI Mean AGBD (Mg/ha)", range = c(0, 400))
plot(r_nyc,  col = hcl.colors(100, "viridis"),
     main = "NYC Mean AGBD (Mg/ha)",  range = c(0, 200))
par(mfrow = c(1, 1))

title: Downloading and Analyzing GEDI L4A Above-Ground Biomass Data
text:
Key Notes

AGBD fill value: Filter out agbd == -9999 before any analysis.
Prediction interval: agbd_pi_lower / agbd_pi_upper give per-footprint 90% uncertainty bounds.
Power beams: BEAM0101, BEAM0110, BEAM1000, BEAM1011 penetrate dense canopy better and yield higher-quality waveforms.
Urban interpretation: GEDI AGBD in cities reflects canopy trees only — not building structure. Near-zero AGBD in NYC corresponds to streets, rooftops, and parking lots.
Version: Always use V002 — it includes updated allometric models and improved algorithm.

title: Radar Datasets
text:
Sentinel-1 — ESA Copernicus
Sentinel-1 provides C-band Synthetic Aperture Radar (SAR) imagery, enabling cloud-penetrating, day-and-night observations of land and ocean surfaces.
Agency: European Space Agency (ESA) — Copernicus Programme Sensor: C-band SAR (5.405 GHz) Spatial resolution: 5 m × 20 m (IW mode, standard) Temporal resolution: ~6-day revisit (combined twin satellites) Polarizations: VV, VH, HH, HV Key applications: Forest above-ground biomass, flood mapping, soil moisture, ice monitoring, subsidence detection






Note



Sentinel-1 data are freely available through the Copernicus Data Space and Google Earth Engine.

title: Radar Datasets
text:
SMAP — Soil Moisture Active Passive (NASA)
SMAP is a NASA satellite mission designed to measure the moisture content of Earth’s soil surface globally and repeatedly. Its L-band radiometer provides the most accurate global soil moisture retrievals currently available from space, and is widely used in hydrology, agriculture, climate modeling, and ecosystem studies.
Agency: NASA Jet Propulsion Laboratory (JPL) Sensor: L-band (1.41 GHz) passive radiometer + (originally active radar, failed 2015) Spatial resolution: ~36 km (radiometer) · 9 km (enhanced product) Temporal resolution: 2–3 day global revisit Launch: January 2015 Key products: - SPL3SMP — Daily global soil moisture (36 km) - SPL3SMP_E — Enhanced daily soil moisture (9 km) - SPL4SMGP — Surface and root-zone soil moisture (9 km, model-assimilated) Key applications: Drought monitoring, flood forecasting, agricultural water use, carbon flux modeling, forest moisture stress






Note



SMAP data are freely available through NASA EarthData and Google Earth Engine.

title: Radar Datasets
text:
ALOS-2 PALSAR-2 — JAXA
ALOS-2 PALSAR-2 is a Japanese L-band SAR satellite operated by JAXA. L-band radar penetrates forest canopy more effectively than C-band, making it particularly valuable for above-ground biomass estimation and forest structure retrieval.
Agency: Japan Aerospace Exploration Agency (JAXA) Sensor: L-band SAR (1.2 GHz) Spatial resolution: 3 m – 100 m (mode dependent) Polarizations: HH, HV, VH, VV (quad-pol available) Key applications: Forest biomass estimation, forest/non-forest mapping, disaster monitoring, wetland mapping






Note



ALOS-2 PALSAR-2 global mosaic data are freely available through JAXA EORC.

title: Radar Datasets
text:
TanDEM-X — DLR
TanDEM-X is a German radar mission that produced a global Digital Elevation Model (DEM) of unprecedented accuracy using X-band InSAR. The global DEM is widely used as a canopy height reference baseline and terrain correction layer.
Agency: German Aerospace Center (DLR) Sensor: X-band SAR (9.65 GHz), bistatic InSAR Spatial resolution: 12 m (global DEM) Vertical accuracy: ~1 m absolute (open terrain) Key applications: Global DEM generation, canopy height estimation, glacier monitoring, terrain analysis






Note



TanDEM-X global DEM data are available through DLR.

title: Radar Datasets
text:
NISAR — NASA / ISRO (Launched 2025)
NISAR (NASA-ISRO Synthetic Aperture Radar) is a joint Earth observation mission between NASA and the Indian Space Research Organisation (ISRO). It is the first dual-frequency SAR satellite ever built, carrying both an L-band (NASA) and an S-band (ISRO) radar. Its primary science goals include measuring ecosystem disturbances, ice-sheet collapse, natural hazards, and sea-level rise. For forest research, NISAR’s L-band radar is expected to provide unprecedented global above-ground biomass and forest disturbance data at high spatial resolution and frequent revisit.
Agency: NASA (Jet Propulsion Laboratory) + ISRO Launch: March 2025 Sensors: L-band SAR (1.25 GHz, NASA) + S-band SAR (2.8 GHz, ISRO) Spatial resolution: ~3–10 m (L-band) · ~3–10 m (S-band) Temporal resolution: 12-day repeat cycle Swath width: 240 km Key applications: Forest above-ground biomass, deforestation and disturbance mapping, wetland dynamics, earthquake and landslide monitoring, glacier flow, sea-level change






Note



NISAR data will be freely available through NASA EarthData and ISRO’s NRSC portal.

title: Radar Datasets
text:
BIOMASS — ESA (Launched 2025)
BIOMASS is ESA’s first P-band SAR satellite, specifically designed to produce the first global maps of forest above-ground biomass. P-band radar (wavelength ~70 cm) penetrates deep into forest canopy and is sensitive to the woody structure of trunks and large branches — the components that store most of the carbon in forests. BIOMASS is a cornerstone mission for global carbon cycle science and will directly support international carbon accounting and climate policy.
Agency: European Space Agency (ESA) — Earth Explorer Mission Launch: April 2025 Sensor: P-band SAR (435 MHz, ~70 cm wavelength), fully polarimetric Spatial resolution: 50 m (biomass product) · ~4.5 m (SAR imagery) Temporal resolution: ~25-day repeat cycle (3 passes per year in tomographic phase) Mission phases: - Tomographic phase (Years 1–3): 3D forest structure mapping using SAR tomography - Interferometric phase (Years 4–5): Change detection and biomass updating Key products: Global forest above-ground biomass density, forest height, forest disturbance Key applications: Forest carbon stock estimation, deforestation monitoring, carbon flux modeling, climate change assessment






Note



BIOMASS data will be freely available through ESA’s Earth Online portal.

text:
USGS 3DEP — Urban Forest Near Central Park, New York City
The datasets shown here are airborne LiDAR point clouds from two open-access programs: the USGS 3D Elevation Program (3DEP), a nationwide topographic mapping initiative, and the NEON Airborne Observation Platform (AOP), which collects high-density ecological LiDAR across NEON field sites. Both programs provide data freely to the public.
Source: USGS 3DEP · NAD83(2011) / UTM Zone 18N Area: ~2.04 km² · Points: 2.21 million · Density: ~1.08 pts/m² Elevation range: −10 m to +385 m (ground to building rooftops)
This tile covers a section of Manhattan adjacent to Central Park. The map below shows the exact footprint of the dataset on a satellite basemap.


The 3D viewer below renders the point cloud colored by elevation. Rotate with left-click, pan with right-click, and scroll to zoom. The tall peaks (orange–red) are Manhattan skyscrapers; the flat ground surface and below-grade infrastructure appear in purple–blue.

Source: NEON Airborne Observation Platform · WGS 84 / UTM Zone 6N Area: ~399 m² · Points: 10.4 thousand · Density: ~26 pts/m² Elevation range: 0 m to 17.3 m (ground to crown top)

title: LiDAR Datasets
text:
GEDI



GEDI (Global Ecosystem Dynamics Investigation) — NASA LiDAR instrument aboard the ISS for measuring forest structure and biomass.


GEDI is a full-waveform LiDAR instrument mounted on the International Space Station. It provides high-resolution measurements of forest vertical structure, canopy height, and above-ground biomass at global scale.
Agency: NASA Goddard Space Flight Center Sensor: Three 1064 nm full-waveform LiDAR lasers Footprint size: ~25 m diameter Along-track spacing: ~60 m · Cross-track spacing: ~600 m Coverage: ~51.6°N to 51.6°S (ISS orbital range) Key products: Canopy height (RH metrics), Plant Area Index (PAI), Above-ground biomass density (AGBD)






Note



GEDI data are freely available through NASA EarthData and Google Earth Engine.

title: LiDAR Datasets
text:
ICESat-2 — NASA
ICESat-2 (Ice, Cloud, and land Elevation Satellite-2) uses a photon-counting LiDAR (ATLAS) to measure surface elevation globally with centimeter-level precision. While primarily designed for ice sheet and sea ice monitoring, ICESat-2 is increasingly used for global forest canopy height estimation and terrain mapping.
Agency: NASA Goddard Space Flight Center Sensor: ATLAS (Advanced Topographic Laser Altimeter System) — 532 nm photon-counting LiDAR Footprint size: ~17 m diameter Along-track spacing: ~0.7 m (photon level) Beam configuration: 3 pairs of strong/weak beams (6 beams total) Temporal resolution: 91-day exact repeat cycle Coverage: Global, up to ±88° latitude Key products: - ATL03 — Global geolocated photons - ATL06 — Land ice surface height - ATL08 — Land and vegetation height (canopy top, terrain) - ATL13 — Inland water surface height Key applications: Forest canopy height, ice sheet mass balance, sea ice freeboard, lake and river water levels, terrain DEM






Note



ICESat-2 data are freely available through NASA EarthData and OpenAltimetry.









Note



USGS 3DEP data are available via the USGS National Map. NEON AOP data are available via the NEON Data Portal. Visualizations produced with lidR, plotly, and leaflet in R.

title: Datasets
text:
FIA — Forest Inventory and Analysis
The USDA Forest Service Forest Inventory and Analysis (FIA) program is the nation’s continuous forest census. FIA plots are systematically distributed across all forested land in the United States and remeasured on a roughly 5–10 year cycle. Each plot records tree species, diameter at breast height (DBH), height, crown class, and site conditions, providing a statistically representative sample of forest composition and structure at national, regional, and state scales.
Source: USDA Forest Service FIA Program Coverage: Contiguous United States, Alaska, Hawaii, and Pacific Islands Key variables: Species, DBH, tree height, basal area, biomass estimates, forest type, ownership






Note



FIA data are freely available through the FIA DataMart.

title: Datasets
text:
NEON — National Ecological Observatory Network
The NEON Terrestrial Observation System collects standardized, long-term ecological data across 81 field sites spanning major climate and vegetation domains in the United States. Vegetation structure data include woody plant cover and height surveys, distributed plot stem maps, and individual tree measurements, designed to align directly with NEON’s airborne LiDAR collections for multi-scale validation.
Source: National Ecological Observatory Network Coverage: 81 sites across 20 eco-climatic domains in the U.S. Key variables: Woody plant percent cover, plant height, stem diameter, species identity, plant phenology






Note



NEON field data are freely available through the NEON Data Portal.









Note



USGS 3DEP data are available via the USGS National Map. NEON AOP data are available via the NEON Data Portal. Visualizations produced with lidR, plotly, and leaflet in R.

title: Optical Remote Sensing Datasets
text:
Landsat — USGS / NASA
Landsat is the longest-running Earth observation satellite program, continuously collecting multispectral imagery since 1972. Operated jointly by USGS and NASA, the program provides a free and open archive essential for long-term land surface change analysis.
Current sensors: Landsat 8 OLI/TIRS · Landsat 9 OLI-2/TIRS-2 Spatial resolution: 30 m (multispectral) · 15 m (panchromatic) · 100 m (thermal) Temporal resolution: 16-day revisit per satellite (~8 days combined) Spectral bands: Coastal/aerosol, Blue, Green, Red, NIR, SWIR1, SWIR2, Panchromatic, Thermal Coverage: Global, continuous since 1972 Key applications: Land cover change, deforestation, urban expansion, agricultural monitoring, wildfire burn severity, surface temperature






Note



Landsat data are freely available through USGS EarthExplorer and Google Earth Engine.

text:
Sentinel-2 — ESA Copernicus
Sentinel-2 is a high-resolution multispectral mission from the European Space Agency (ESA) under the Copernicus Earth Observation Programme. Its combination of high spatial resolution, frequent revisit time, and free data access has made it one of the most widely used satellites in vegetation and land surface research.
Sensors: MultiSpectral Instrument (MSI) — Sentinel-2A and Sentinel-2B Spatial resolution: 10 m (B2, B3, B4, B8) · 20 m (B5, B6, B7, B8A, B11, B12) · 60 m (B1, B9, B10) Temporal resolution: ~5-day revisit (combined twin satellites) Spectral bands: 13 bands from visible to SWIR, including red-edge bands for vegetation analysis Coverage: Global land surface Key applications: Forest canopy health, LAI estimation, crop monitoring, urban green space mapping, water body detection






Note



Sentinel-2 data are freely available through the Copernicus Data Space and Google Earth Engine.

title: Optical Remote Sensing Datasets
text:
MODIS — NASA Terra & Aqua
MODIS (Moderate Resolution Imaging Spectroradiometer) is a key instrument aboard NASA’s Terra and Aqua satellites. While its spatial resolution is coarser than Landsat or Sentinel-2, its near-daily global coverage and long record (since 1999) make it indispensable for large-scale vegetation dynamics, land surface temperature, and fire monitoring.
Agency: NASA Goddard Space Flight Center Sensors: MODIS aboard Terra (EOS AM-1) and Aqua (EOS PM-1) Spatial resolution: 250 m (bands 1–2) · 500 m (bands 3–7) · 1000 m (bands 8–36) Temporal resolution: Daily global coverage (1–2 days revisit) Spectral bands: 36 bands from visible to thermal infrared (0.4–14.4 μm) Record length: Terra since February 2000 · Aqua since July 2002 Key products: - MOD13 / MYD13 — Vegetation indices (NDVI, EVI) at 250 m / 500 m / 1 km - MOD15 — Leaf Area Index (LAI) and FPAR - MOD17 — Gross/Net Primary Production (GPP/NPP) - MOD44B — Vegetation continuous fields (tree cover, non-tree, bare ground) - MCD64A1 — Monthly burned area - MOD11 — Land surface temperature and emissivity Key applications: Global vegetation phenology, drought monitoring, wildfire detection, land cover classification, carbon flux estimation, urban heat islands






Note



MODIS data are freely available through NASA EarthData and Google Earth Engine.

title: Downloading and Analyzing GEDI L2A Relative Height Metrics
text:
GEDI L2A (Global Ecosystem Dynamics Investigation, Level 2A) provides footprint-level relative height (RH) metrics derived from full-waveform LiDAR. Unlike L4A which estimates above-ground biomass density, L2A reports the vertical distribution of returned energy — directly measuring canopy height structure.







Metric
Meaning




RH25
Height below which 25% of waveform energy is returned


RH50
Median canopy height


RH75
Height below which 75% of energy is returned


RH95
Upper canopy height (~95th percentile) — most used as canopy height estimate


RH98
Near-maximum canopy height


RH100
Maximum height of any return



This tutorial applies the same workflow as GEDI L4A to two contrasting landscapes:

Setup

install.packages(c("rGEDI", "hdf5r", "sf", "terra",
                   "ggplot2", "dplyr", "tidyr", "leaflet",
                   "viridis", "patchwork"))


library(hdf5r); library(sf);      library(terra)
library(ggplot2); library(dplyr); library(tidyr)
library(leaflet); library(viridis); library(patchwork); library(scales)

title: Downloading and Analyzing GEDI L2A Relative Height Metrics
text:
Step 1 — Define Two Study Areas

scbi <- list(
  name    = "NEON SCBI — Front Royal, VA",
  lon_min = -78.20, lat_min = 38.85,
  lon_max = -78.10, lat_max = 38.95
)

nyc <- list(
  name    = "Central Park & surroundings — New York City",
  lon_min = -74.05, lat_min = 40.70,
  lon_max = -73.85, lat_max = 40.85
)

region_to_sf <- function(r) {
  st_bbox(c(xmin = r$lon_min, ymin = r$lat_min,
            xmax = r$lon_max, ymax = r$lat_max),
          crs = 4326) |> st_as_sfc() |> st_as_sf()
}

The map below shows GEDI orbital track coverage (green lines) and both study areas (red bounding boxes). Ascending (SW→NE) and descending (NW→SE) passes cross due to the ISS orbital inclination of ~51.6°.

title: Downloading and Analyzing GEDI L2A Relative Height Metrics
text:
Step 2 — Find GEDI L2A Granules

library(httr); library(jsonlite)

gedi_finder <- function(r, product = "GEDI02_A") {
  url  <- paste0("https://lpdaacsvc.cr.usgs.gov/services/gedifinder",
                 "?product=", product, "&version=002",
                 "&bbox=", r$lon_min, ",", r$lat_min,
                 ",",      r$lon_max, ",", r$lat_max)
  fromJSON(content(GET(url), "text"))$data
}

scbi_granules <- gedi_finder(scbi)
nyc_granules  <- gedi_finder(nyc)

cat("SCBI granules:", length(scbi_granules), "\n")
cat("NYC  granules:", length(nyc_granules),  "\n")

title: Downloading and Analyzing GEDI L2A Relative Height Metrics
text:
Step 3 — Download Granules
Requires a free NASA EarthData account (urs.earthdata.nasa.gov).

library(rGEDI)
gediDownload(filepath = scbi_granules, outdir = "data/gedi_l2a_scbi")
gediDownload(filepath = nyc_granules,  outdir = "data/gedi_l2a_nyc")


Each L2A granule is ~300 MB–1 GB. For a small bounding box, 1–3 granules typically suffice.

Step 5 — Quality Filtering

quality_filter <- function(df) {
  df |> filter(quality_flag == 1, degrade_flag == 0,
               rh95 >= 0, rh95 < 100)
}

scbi_clean <- quality_filter(scbi_raw)
nyc_clean  <- quality_filter(nyc_raw)

title: Downloading and Analyzing GEDI L2A Relative Height Metrics
text:
Results

Spatial Distribution of RH95


SCBI shows uniformly tall canopy (RH95 20–40 m) consistent with mature temperate forest. NYC reveals a sharp spatial contrast: the Central Park core reaches 15–25 m, while surrounding urban pixels drop to near zero where impervious surfaces dominate.




RH95 Frequency Distribution


SCBI follows a near-normal distribution centred around 28 m. NYC shows a strongly bimodal pattern — a large mode below 5 m (streets, rooftops) and a secondary peak around 15–25 m (park trees).




Relative Height Profile — RH25 to RH98


The RH profile reveals canopy vertical structure. SCBI’s wide spread from RH25 to RH95 indicates a multi-layered forest with understory. NYC’s RH values remain low across all percentiles outside the park, reflecting sparse or absent canopy.




NYC Detail — Central Park vs Urban Surroundings

nyc_labeled <- nyc_clean |>
  mutate(land_type = ifelse(
    lon >= -73.981 & lon <= -73.949 & lat >= 40.764 & lat <= 40.800,
    "Central Park (Green Space)", "Urban Surroundings"
  ))





Canopy Vertical Structure — RH50 vs RH95


The steeper RH50–RH95 slope in SCBI indicates a top-heavy canopy (closed overstory, open understory), while NYC shows a shallower, more compressed relationship — canopy is both lower and more uniformly distributed vertically.

section: Step 6 — Rasterize RH95 to 500 m Grid
text:
Step 6 — Rasterize RH95 to 500 m Grid

rasterize_rh <- function(df, region, field = "rh95", res = 0.0045) {
  r_tmpl <- rast(xmin = region$lon_min, xmax = region$lon_max,
                 ymin = region$lat_min, ymax = region$lat_max,
                 resolution = res, crs = "EPSG:4326")
  vect(df, geom = c("lon", "lat"), crs = "EPSG:4326") |>
    rasterize(r_tmpl, field = field, fun = "mean")
}

r_scbi_rh95 <- rasterize_rh(scbi_clean, scbi)
r_nyc_rh95  <- rasterize_rh(nyc_clean,  nyc)

par(mfrow = c(1, 2))
plot(r_scbi_rh95, col = hcl.colors(100, "plasma"),
     main = "SCBI — Mean RH95 (m)", range = c(0, 45))
plot(r_nyc_rh95,  col = hcl.colors(100, "plasma"),
     main = "NYC  — Mean RH95 (m)", range = c(0, 30))
par(mfrow = c(1, 1))

title: Downloading and Analyzing GEDI L2A Relative Height Metrics
text:
Key Notes

RH95 as canopy height: RH95 is the most widely used canopy height proxy from GEDI L2A, more stable than RH100 which is sensitive to noise returns.
Coordinate system: WGS84 (EPSG:4326) for all coordinates.
RH array indexing: In the HDF5 file, rh is 0-indexed — rh[96] = RH95, rh[51] = RH50, etc.
Quality flag: L2A uses quality_flag (not l4_quality_flag as in L4A). Keep only shots where quality_flag == 1.
Urban canopy: Low RH values in urban areas do not mean no trees — they reflect the average canopy height including large fractions of impervious surface within the ~25 m footprint.
Version: Always use V002 for the most accurate waveform decomposition algorithm.
